caption:
Optical imagery is blind during rainy season. That is the exact season floods and cover-dependent movement happen.

A camera, airborne or orbital, needs a clear line of sight and daylight. Cloud cover, smoke, and haze block the wavelength it depends on. Over West Africa in peak monsoon months, usable optical frames across a flood-prone reach can be sparse for weeks at a stretch.

Synthetic-aperture radar uses a longer wavelength that cloud does not stop, and it generates its own illumination, so it works at night. It is not a sharper camera — it is a different physical principle, chosen because the gap in optical coverage falls precisely when the risk is highest.

The trade: radar imagery reads differently than a photograph and takes more interpretation to turn into a confirmed call. That cost is why both have a role in a collection plan.

card.headline: Cloud stops a camera. It doesn't stop radar.
card.sub: Synthetic-aperture radar uses a wavelength cloud does not block, and lights its own scene — built for the exact season when optical imagery goes blind.

rationale: Delivers a concrete, non-repeated physics lesson (why radar beats cloud cover) that builds operator literacy without touching any banned claims or prior angles.
